sentences.text:
Counsel for Petitioner :- Vivek Saran Counsel for Respondent :- C.S.C.,Shiv Prakash Gupta Hon'ble Mahesh Chandra Tripathi,J.
Hon'ble Manjive Shukla,J.
1. Heard Shri Vivek Saran, learned counsel for the petitioners, learned Standing Counsel for the State respondent no.1 and Shri Shiv Prakash Gupta, learned counsel for Meerut Development Authority, Meerut (respondent nos.2 and 3).
2.

The instant writ petition has been preferred inter-alia for the following reliefs:-
"(i) Issue a writ, order or direction in the nature of mandamus commanding the respondents not to interfere in the peaceful possession and enjoyment of the property of the petitioners bearing Municipal/House No.137, Jamunanagar, Meerut erstwhile Ajay Kumar And 2 Others vs State Of Up And 2 Others on 3 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/193719734/
1 part of Khasra No.403, Village Kazipur, District Meerut.

entities.text: Ajay Kumar And 2 Others vs State Of Up And 2 Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Learned counsel for the petitioners submits that the State Government published a notification under Section 4 of Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (in short, the Act) on 14.08.1987 acquiring land of Villages Kazipur, Budhera, Jahidpur and Ghosipur, District Meerut including Khasra No.403 situated in Village Kazipur, which was recorded in the name of the grandfather of the petitioners late Jai Karan and he was also having his abadi on an area of 600 sq. mtrs. over the land in question.
He has placed reliance on the survey report, wherein the disputed site was mentioned as abadi land.
He further states that till date, the petitioners have not been dispossessed from their holding and they have every right to press the relief for de-notification under Section 48 of the Act.
4. The relief is resisted by learned counsel for the respondents on the premise that admittedly, the present dispute relates to Arazi No.403 area 2-8-5 bigha.
The notification under Section 4 read with Section 17 (1) and Section 6 read with Section 17 (4) of the Act were issued on 14.08.1987 and 04.09.1987 respectively.
Later on, the Competent Authority had taken over the possession of the disputed land on 31.03.1989 and the award was made on 22.02.1990.
The urgency was invoked under Section 17 of the Act and the enquiry under Section 5A of the Act was dispensed with.

He submits that once the possession was taken over, the land has vested in the State Government absolutely free from all encumbrances then the application under Section 48 of the Act could not be pressed.

5. Learned counsel for the respondents fairly states that even in view of the award, the compensation was deposited and if the original owner had not lifted the compensation, the petitioners, if entitled, may approach the Special Land Acquisition Officer for the disbursement of compensation, if there are no legal impediments.

He further submits that it is settled law that after the notification under Section 4 (1) is published in the Gazette, any encumbrance created by the owner does not bind the Government, and the purchaser does not acquire any title to the property.
Admittedly, power under Section 17(4) of the Act was exercised dispensing with the enquiry under Section 5A and on service of the notice under Section 9 of the Act, the possession was taken.
Consequently, the land vested in the State, free from all encumbrances.

In support of his submission, he has placed reliance on the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in V. Chandrasekaran & Ors. vs. The Administrative Officer & Ors., (2012) 12 SCC 133.
6.

entities.text: V. Chandrasekaran & Ors. vs. The Administrative Officer & Ors., (2012) 12 SCC 133
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Heard rival submissions and perused the record.
7. We have occasion to examine the record in question and find that the State Government initiated acquisition proceedings in the year 1987 for planned development.
As per instruction, which is categorical, certain piece of land of petitioners' grand-father was acquired and the award was made on 22.02.1990.

The Competent Authority had also taken over actual physical possession of the Ajay Kumar And 2 Others vs State Of Up And 2 Others on 3 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/193719734/
2 acquired land on 31.03.1989.

entities.text: Ajay Kumar And 2 Others vs State Of Up And 2 Others
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The land in dispute stood vested in the State, free from all encumbrances.

8. In V. Chandrasekaran & Ors. vs. The Administrative Officer & Ors. (supra), the Apex Court has held that after the issuance of a notification under Section 4 of the Act, 1894, a purchaser has no right to challenge the acquisition but is entitled to compensation as he steps into the shoes of the original landowner.

entities.text: V. Chandrasekaran & Ors. vs. The Administrative Officer & Ors
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
The relevant paragraph of the judgment is reproduced below:
"18.

In view of the above, the law on the issue can be summarized to the effect that a person who purchases land subsequent to the issuance of a Section 4 notification with respect to it, is not competent to challenge the validity of the acquisition proceedings on any ground whatsoever, for the reason that the sale deed executed in his favour does not confer upon him, any title and at the most he can claim compensation on the basis of his vendor's title."

9. A similar view was taken by the Apex Court in U.P. Jal Nigam v. M/s. Kalra Properties Pvt. Ltd.,
(1996) 3 SCC 124, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court held that a sale made after the publication of the notification under Section 4(1) of the Act, 1894, is void against the State.

entities.text:
U.P. Jal Nigam v. M/s. Kalra Properties Pvt. Ltd.,
(1996) 3 SCC 124
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In that case, M/s. Kalra Properties had no right, title, or interest in the land and could not challenge the validity of the notification or the acquisition.

It was held that any encumbrance created after the notification under Section 4(1) does not bind the Government, and the purchaser is merely entitled to claim compensation, stepping into the shoes of the original owner.
10.
Considering the factual situation, which emerges from the record, we are not inclined to proceed further in the matter.
Needless to say that in case, the petitioners claim compensation, they can press the relief before the competent authority.
11. With the aforesaid observations, the instant writ petition stands disposed off.
